https://www.dw.com/en/pakistan-suicide-b.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5I9tq Hundreds of people protesting increased militant violence were present when the attacker detonated his suicide vest Image: Sherin Zada/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement A suicide bomber killed 14 people and injured dozens more in an attack targeting anti-militancy demonstrators in the city of Kabal in Pakistan 's northwestern Swat Valley. Five police officers were among those killed at the event, which was staged outside a local police station to protest growing militant violence in the region and the state's inability to protect citizens. Those gathered accused authorities of failing to act decisively against militants , saying residents want to live without fear after years of devastating violence. The area was the home of Nobel laureate Malala Yousafzai , who was shot there by a Taliban gunman in 2012. Hundreds of people were at the rally and social media video footage showed a speaker mid-sentence when an explosion rocked the area and sparked panic among demonstrators. "The suicide bomber blew himself up when asked for a search in front of the police station," a local police official said. No group has claimed responsibility for the crime. A former Taliban stronghold President Asif Ali Zardari and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif both condemned the attack. "Terrorists," said Zardari, "will never succeed in their nefarious efforts to harm peace, national unity and the writ of the state." Pakistan has experienced a surge in militant attacks of late, with many targeting police and security forces. The Swat Valley was a Taliban stronghold between 2007 and 2009, when Pakistan's military drove the Islamists out and re-established government control over the area. The religious militants have recently resurfaced, however, with the Pakistani Taliban , known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, being particularly active. The TTP is separate from, but allied with, Afghanistan's Taliban rulers and has been a source of tension between the neighboring countries. Pakistan says the TTP and other militant groups are carrying out attacks in the country with the support of Afghanistan's Taliban rulers and has promised to continue targeting the TTP and its support network. http://www.batonrougepost.com/news/27924.text: Latvia wants EU billions for its anti-Russia policies RT.com 18 Aug 2026, 01:34 GMT+10 Riga says lost trade and surging military spending have left the Baltic state carrying an outsized financial burden Latvia wants Brussels to provide billions in additional funding as lost trade with Russia and soaring military spending put growing pressure on the Baltic state's finances, Politico reported on Monday. Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs told the outlet that he has asked Brussels to provide €7 billion ($8.2 billion) under the EU's next seven-year budget, on top of other funding already earmarked for Latvia. The sum would cover almost half of Riga's projected €15.1 billion ($17.3 billion) military spending bill for 2028-2034. Kulbergs said that Latvia is taking on debt to finance what its government views as security spending benefiting the rest of Europe. "We are getting our budget deficit to the maximum," he told Politico, saying Latvia is borrowing to pay for "the defense of the whole of Europe." Latvia has been one of the EU's strongest advocates of sanctions on Russia and has steadily dismantled trade, transport and energy links with its eastern neighbor since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022. The policies, however, have led to a significant economic decline across the region. Politico reported last year that cross-border trade with Russia had "largely collapsed" across the Baltic states, while tourism and investment had also declined, prompting Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia to seek additional financial aid from Brussels. The costs of Riga's anti-Russian policies have since become a major campaign issue ahead of Latvia's October 3 parliamentary election. Opposition politician Ainars Slesers has insisted that Riga should demand compensation in return for backing further EU sanctions. "We are losing money ... we are talking about how to support Ukraine, but we are a victim," he told Politico, adding that economic ties with Russia should eventually be restored. Despite seeking billions from Brussels to offset the fallout, Kulbergs has called for even tougher measures against Moscow, including a total EU visa ban for Russian citizens and renewed attempts to use frozen Russian sovereign assets for Ukraine. Russia has long argued that the Baltic states have devastated their own economies by dismantling previously profitable ties while sharply increasing military spending over what their governments describe as a potential threat from Russia. Moscow has repeatedly denied having plans to attack the Baltic states or other NATO members, dismissing such claims as "nonsense" and Russophobic fearmongering intended to justify inflated military budgets to taxpayers, while warning that European nations are preparing for a full-scale war against Russia. https://www.asiaone.com/world/germany-bl.text: world Germany blames Russia for last month's attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport Ukrainian Antonov aircrafts are parked behind a fence on the grounds of Leipzig/Halle Airport, where investigations are underway following the drone incident that occurred early Wednesday morning, in Schkeuditz, Germany, Aug 6. PHOTO: Associated Press PUBLISHED ON September 02, 2026 2:02 AM BERLIN —The German government on Tuesday (Sept 1) blamed Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month using a drone laden with explosives, and announced that it would shut down a Russian consulate among other measures. The drone was found near a Ukrainian plane on Aug 4 and the device was defused. German officials said at the time that the incident posed a new level of danger. Moscow has been widely accused by Western officials of running a campaign of sabotage and disruption with the aim of undermining support for Ukraine and destabilizing European nations. Minister says evidence points to a familiar pattern German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said authorities found elements such as the drone configuration, components, explosives and detonator that are "known to us from other Russian hybrid operations and its war against Ukraine". He said the device pointed to "a high degree of technical expertise" and painstaking planning, but carrying out the plan appears to have been left to "low-level" agents. Dobrindt told reporters that intelligence points to "people being involved who acted on behalf of Russian state entities", though he didn't specify which ones. "Taken together, the police investigations, the pattern and intelligence findings prove a Russian responsibility for the attempted attack at Leipzig airport." Germany will shut a Russian consulate Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said that "with the attempted attack in Leipzig, the Russian leadership decided deliberately to do significant damage again to our already massively burdened bilateral relationship". He said the Russian consulate in Bonn will be closed effective Sept 18. The Russian House cultural centre in Berlin also will be closed, though that may take some time. Germany will propose the addition of more people from Russia to EU sanctions lists "in the context of hybrid attacks", step up entry controls for people from Russia and increase "pressure on the shadow fleet", a reference to tankers suspected of shipping Russian oil in violation of international sanctions, Wadephul said. The EU has sanctioned hundreds of "shadow fleet" ships. The Russian ambassador was summoned to the foreign ministry in Berlin. Wadephul later told ARD television that "Germany can at any time show a stronger reaction, (but) that is not necessary at this point". Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said there would be a "fitting response" to the planned closures, Russian state news agency Tass reported. She rejected claims of Russian involvement in the attempted drone attack, calling them a "far-fetched and contrived pretext" for Berlin to escalate tensions and arguing that "as usual, no convincing or serious evidence has been presented whatsoever". Russian President Vladimir Putin dismissed Berlin's allegations, instead claiming that Germany's leadership sought to use the incident to distract from their own failings and dissatisfaction among voters with "the need to counter an aggressive Russia". "But where is the proof? Well, the proof has been planted," Putin told reporters in the early hours of Wednesday in Kyrgyzstan, where he attended a summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation. He didn't elaborate on why he thinks the proof has been planted, nor did he offer evidence. Around 200 incidents blamed on Russia Leipzig/Halle is a major hub for international freight and for providing support to Ukraine. The planes that regularly use it include Ukrainian Antonov transport aircraft. It is also home to NATO's Strategic Airlift International Solution, or SALIS, which is currently operational almost every day in delivering equipment to NATO battle groups along its eastern flank from Finland to Romania and supporting EU and alliance nation missions. In 2024, an incendiary device ignited at a logistics centre at the airport and set fire to a freight container before it could be loaded onto a cargo plane, part of a plot that Western security officials suspect was organised by Russian intelligence. The Associated Press has tracked around 200 incidents of sabotage and malign activity across Europe blamed on Russia by Western officials since the invasion of Ukraine. That includes organising plots to set fire to warehouses, launching drones and trying to kill enemies abroad as well as stealing defence technology and carrying out cyberattacks on critical European infrastructure. In May, Putin responded to the AP findings and said Moscow is not waging a sabotage campaign against Europe. He demanded that AP "name one proven fact". Russia has faced many packages of EU sanctions The EU has slapped almost two dozen packages of sanctions on Russia over its war in Ukraine, targeting roughly 3,000 people and entities. EU foreign ministers will meet in Ireland Wednesday. European allies rallied around Germany after Tuesday's announcement. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said in a post on X that he had spoken with Chancellor Friedrich Merz and "NATO stands in full solidarity with Germany after the Russian hybrid attack in Leipzig." In mid-August, the German Cabinet approved plans to give the country's intelligence services broader powers for actions such as disabling sabotage and hacking attempts. The planned reform, which had been in the works for months, still requires parliamentary approval. Hours before Tuesday's German statement, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, who has frequently warned that Russia is carrying out a campaign of sabotage against NATO countries, said Poland has been targeted by new acts of sabotage including arson within the past "dozens of hours." He spoke the day after a fire broke out at WB Electronics, which the Polish government has described as Europe's biggest drone manufacturer. Prosecutors said Monday they launched an investigation based on suspicions of the "participation of foreign intelligence activities against the Republic of Poland", without elaborating on what country might be responsible. They said the fire in Skarżysko-Kamienna destroyed warehouse facilities and caused damage estimated at at least 15 million zlotys (S$5 million). https://www.perthnow.com.au/entertainmen.text: Lesley Manville battles spies, political violence and the freezing streets of Cold War Warsaw in her new thriller Winter of the Crow. The actress, 70, stars as British psychiatry professor Joan Andrews in director Kasia Adamik’s upcoming drama, which Cohen Media Group will release in US cinemas on October 9. Inspired by Nobel Prize-winning author Olga Tokarczuk’s short story Professor Andrews Goes to Warsaw, the film follows Joan after she arrives in Poland as a guest lecturer in December 1981, only to become trapped when martial law is imposed and the country effectively shuts down overnight. Joan is carrying a Polaroid camera when she witnesses the secret police committing a brutal murder. With Poland sealed off and her own life in danger, she goes into hiding and becomes a fugitive while attempting to navigate a Warsaw transformed by repression and violence. The cast also includes Tom Burke, who starred in Furiosa: A Mad Max Saga and The Souvenir, Andrzej Konopka, Sascha Ley and Zofia Wichłacz. Kasia was quoted by Variety saying: “Winter of the Crow is deeply personal to me, and I wanted to capture the fear and uncertainty of a moment when everyday life could change in an instant. Lesley Manville brings such intelligence, strength and humanity to Joan, and I’m thrilled that audiences will have the opportunity to experience her extraordinary performance – and this story – on the big screen.” The movie marks another major role for Lesley during a particularly busy period in her five-decade stage and screen career. She won the 2026 Tony Award for best performance by an actress in a leading role in a play for portraying Jocasta opposite Mark Strong in Robert Icke’s production of Oedipus on Broadway. The production had previously earned Lesley her second Olivier Award when it was staged in London. Lesley subsequently appeared at London’s National Theatre in Les Liaisons Dangereuses alongside Monica Barbaro and Aidan Turner, with Marianne Elliott directing Christopher Hampton’s adaptation. She is also set to return to the West End in 2027 opposite Anna Maxwell Martin in a revival of Tracy Letts’ August: Osage County at the Noël Coward Theatre. Lesley will play Violet Weston, with Anna appearing as her daughter Barbara Fordham and Jeremy Herrin directing. Her best-known screen performances include Cyril Woodcock in Paul Thomas Anderson’s Phantom Thread, which earned her an Academy Award nomination, and Princess Margaret in the final two seasons of Netflix royal drama The Crown, for which she received an Emmy nomination. Lesley has also starred in Mrs. Harris Goes to Paris, Magpie Murders, Moonflower Murders, Sherwood, Back to Black and Mike Leigh’s Another Year. Winter of the Crow is directed by Kasia from a screenplay by Sandra Buchta, Kasia and Lucinda Coxon, with Olga Chajdas, Stanisław Dziedzic, Katarzyna Ozga, Nicolas Steil and Samantha Taylor producing. Robert Aaronson, executive vice president of Cohen Media Group, said: “Anchored by a remarkable performance from Lesley Manville, Kasia Adamik has created a film that is both a gripping thriller and a deeply human story.” He added: “The screenplay truly captures the uncertainty and tension of this pivotal moment in history. We’re very proud to bring it to theaters this October.”
